```{python}
class InterventionPreTriggerWindow:
    """Pre-trigger window that reaches back past the design takeover."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced p90 take-over time + transport)
    t_pre = AISLE.pre_trigger_window  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    headroom = (t_pre - t_ool).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_pre >= t_ool, "The window must reach back past the design takeover.")
    check(abs(t_pre.to(second).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"pre-trigger window: {t_pre}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ool_str = fmt_latency(t_ool, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_pre_str = fmt_latency(t_pre, unit=second, precision=0)
```

Upon receiving an intervention trigger (such as an operator takeover, an emergency stop trip, or an enforcer barrier violation), the logger freezes a configured **pre-trigger window** ($T_{\text{pre}} =$ `{python} InterventionPreTriggerWindow.t_pre_str`) and transitions to recording a dedicated post-trigger segment. The window is the `{python} InterventionPreTriggerWindow.t_ool_str` design out-of-loop takeover of @sec-intervention-reaction-drift rounded up to whole seconds, because the operator's response alone spans that interval after the divergence has begun; a site that measures a longer takeover tail must lengthen it. Missing frames or overwritten samples remain declared gaps in the pre-intervention evidence. If the buffer only recorded data from the instant of human physical contact, the telemetry would capture the recovery while completely discarding the anomalous proposals and perception states that made the rescue necessary. Capturing the pre-trigger interval preserves the learner-visited failure states required for DAgger relabeling and root-cause model evaluation.

Append-only hash chains support detection of later log modification when their anchors and keys remain protected. Within the Nervous System, logging routines batch evidence tuples into fixed blocks corresponding to $100\text{ ms}$ of physical execution. Each block is hashed using SHA-256, and its digest is concatenated with the hash of the preceding block to form an append-only cryptographic chain:
$$H_k = \text{SHA-256}\left( H_{k-1} \,\|\, \text{Block}_k \right).$$
The SHA-256 links are unkeyed; an attacker who can rewrite the entire chain can recompute them. Periodic authenticated anchors in protected storage provide the external integrity reference. An eMMC Replay Protected Memory Block (RPMB) supplies authenticated, replay-protected writes under its key and counter rules; it is rewritable storage, not a battery-backed or write-once medium. The threat model must protect the anchoring credentials and identify which prefix an anchor authenticates. An unanchored tail and a missing block remain evidence gaps.

## The Authority Record {#sec-intervention-authority-log}

An investigator who asks, weeks after the blocked-aisle takeover, who was driving the base as it neared the rack end has only what the machine recorded. Emitting the **authority record**\index{Authority record!definition}, the twelfth record in the record chain, bridges supervisory arbitration with downstream verification and release claims. The record consumes two upstream contracts from Part III: from the enforcement record of @sec-enforcement-telemetry it takes the rungs of the fallback ladder, so every fallback it logs names the rung the permission path executed; from the placement record of @sec-placement-hardware-allocation it takes the measured timing and bus allocations of the operator-input path. It synthesizes two core deliverables of its own: The static authority manifest, the capability matrix of @sec-intervention-human-authority in machine-checkable form, binds every actuator channel to its authorized actors, operational preconditions, preemption tiers, and transition deadlines, and it is loaded and verified before the actuator drivers energize. The per-tick **authority log**\index{Authority log} is a separate stream that records, for every tick, who held authority and what was proposed, admitted, and delivered, so that a tick without an entry reads as a gap, never as an implied pass; neither part substitutes for the other.

### The static authority manifest and capability binding {#sec-intervention-manifest-binding}

The static authority manifest supplies the configuration against which the recorded decisions are judged. Loading and sealing it before operation binds each event to the permissions and limits that were in force.

The static authority manifest specifies every permitted interaction as a hard contract between the physical platform and its potential operators. Each entry identifies a distinct physical authority domain through a hardware actuator mask, an authorized entity class (such as a local physical operator, a remote teleoperation console, an autonomous trajectory policy, or an emergency stop loop), and an integer **preemption tier**\index{Preemption tier}. An entity presenting a command vector must prove its authority through cryptographic role credentials verified by the permission path before its input can enter the actuation pipeline. A network operator's command arrives as an OPERATOR payload under the proposal header of @sec-nervous-cadences, carrying the operator's role, the requested channel mask, the command, a nonce, and a keyed tag. Alongside the credential, the entry specifies the single-writer mutual exclusion policy for the channel, the maximum execution-lease duration, $T_{\text{lease,man}}$ for an operator (bounding the silence tolerated before revocation and state-dependent fallback), the command rate ceiling $r$ (how rapidly a requested command may change), the active blending duration $\tau_{\text{blend}}$ enforcing a $C^2$ bumpless authority transfer ramp to maintain the kinodynamic feasibility bounds established in @sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility, and the terminal fallback state that the hardware enters if an active session is severed.

Each per-tick entry of the authority log carries the full evidence tuple defined in @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs: the hardware event timestamp $t_{\text{MCU}}$ on the safety microcontroller's clock, the actuator channels the decision applies to, the authority state $S_{\text{auth}}$ (`AUTO`, `PEND`, `BLEND`, `MAN`, `FALLBACK` with its ladder rung, or `PROTECTIVE`, codes for the six states of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions), the authenticated operator role $\text{ID}_{\text{operator}}$, the remaining execution-lease duration $T_{\text{lease,rem}}$, the cause of any preemption, the blend factor $\alpha(t)$ of the enforcer-owned profile, the proposed, admitted, and delivered commands ($\mathbf{u}_{\text{prop}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{enf}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{act}}$), the sampled plant state $\mathbf{x}_{\text{state}}$, and the hash link to the preceding block, authenticated through the protected anchoring scheme. The versioned static manifest supplies vector units, field order, the clock mapping and its error bound, credential rules, and hardware access controls.

::: {.column-margin}
**Byte layout:** The authority record's fields, types, and offsets are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-authority.
:::

### Per-tick evidence tuples and the fault injection suite {#sec-intervention-evidence-tuples}

Verification draws its test inputs from the static manifest and its evidence from the event schema. The manifest's `authority_claims` field hands @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list four authority rules by identifier, each of which becomes a hardware-in-the-loop fault case on the machine:

- **A1.** Exactly one qualified enforcer output path writes each actuator channel. Source arbitration and hardware access controls prevent a second sender from bypassing that path while the policy and remote assistant both propose commands; successful bus arbitration alone does not satisfy this claim.
- **A2.** No lower-tier source bypasses an active higher-tier source or the independent permission check. An autonomous policy proposal during `MAN` is ignored, and an assistant command that opposes the enforcer's admitted barrier limit is clamped or rejected.
- **A3.** An unacknowledged handover or stalled manual lease strictly decays authority by $T_{\text{timeout}}$ of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions, initiating controlled fallback by the earlier of the configured lease ceiling and the clearance-derived deadline of @eq-intervention-latest-fallback, whose partial-budget upper bound is `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.t_latest_in_str` at the `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.v_in_str` slow-down before an in-loop takeover and `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.t_latest_str` for a handover the policy requests at the `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.v_aisle_str` aisle speed. Both are additional-delay allocations in the capture-origin ledger. The live deadline uses the actual event history and only future delay, with no repeated charge for elapsed capture-to-admission travel.
- **A4.** The enforcer rejects a replayed `veto_path`, `manual_drive`, or `accept_item` packet, or one with an invalid authentication tag or expired sequence counter, without changing still-valid channel authority. It records the rejection in the evidence tuple; the active lease continues aging.

The authority rules make the event record testable. The same timestamps also identify which controller produced each segment of a recovery, a distinction required before those segments can become learning targets.

### Causal masking and recovery eligibility {#sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility}

When logging intervention episodes for downstream policy retraining, the recording system must enforce **causal intervention masking**\index{Causal intervention masking}. In imitation learning and dataset aggregation architectures, the optimization objective over recorded telemetry trajectories is formulated as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{imitation}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}^*, \mathcal{M}) \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{H} \mathcal{M}(t) \cdot \ell\left(\pi_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t), \mathbf{u}^*(t)\right) \right]$$ {#eq-intervention-causal-masking-loss}
where $\ell(\pi_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t), \mathbf{u}^*(t))$ is the policy prediction loss (such as MSE across action chunks or score-matching denoising loss for diffusion policies), $\mathcal{M}(t) \in \{0, 1\}$ is a binary causal mask, and $\mathbf{u}^*(t)$ is the training target. The training set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ is built from the log, not copied from it. Each logged state keeps its place, but its target and mask are assigned by the interval it falls in, so the logged command need not be the target. The safety microcontroller's timestamped authority transitions identify controller ownership; measured stabilization, review of task validity, and the availability of an expert label determine which samples receive $\mathcal{M}(t) = 1$ and with which target.

A supervisory intervention event does not represent a monolithic demonstration. Instead, it spans four mathematically distinct temporal intervals along the physical timeline:

1. **Compounding policy drift ($t_{\text{div}} \le t < t_{\text{commit}}$)**: The autonomous policy $\pi_\theta$ drifts away from the expert distribution, potentially accumulating compounding error (@sec-data-policy-coverage) while the operator perceives, orients, and decides (the pre-commit interval of @eq-intervention-reaction-floor).
   - *Masking policy*: The autonomous proposals $\hat{\mathbf{u}}(t)$ executed during this drift are never targets; training on them teaches the policy to reproduce its own failure trajectories. Without an expert label, $\mathcal{M}(t) = 0$.
   - *DAgger & relabeling utility*: Crucially, the *learner-visited states* $\mathbf{x}(t)$ must not be discarded. In dataset aggregation algorithms such as DAgger [@ross2011reduction] and its human-gated variants (@sec-data-intervention-recovery), these off-distribution states are precisely the high-leverage samples needed to mitigate covariate shift. When an expert policy or human annotator supplies a corrective action for such a state, the sample enters training with $\mathcal{M}(t) = 1$ and the new target $\mathbf{u}^*(t) = \pi^*(\mathbf{x}_t)$, teaching the network how to recover back to nominal execution. The state stays; only its label changes. When no expert can supply that label, which is common for continuous control, the state keeps $\mathcal{M}(t) = 0$ and remains in the record for failure analysis and later relabeling.
2. **Atomic handover and enforcer blend ($t_{\text{commit}} \le t < t_{\text{commit}} + \tau_{\text{blend}}$)**: The safety microcontroller latches endpoints and executes the $C^2$ smoothstep trajectory.
   - *Masking policy*: $\mathcal{M}(t) = 0$ unconditionally. Dispatched setpoints $\mathbf{u}(t)$ are synthetic interpolation splines generated by the enforcer's deterministic quintic profile. They reflect neither neural policy intent nor human cognitive demonstration. Training on this interval teaches the policy to output ungrounded, open-loop kinematic ramps.
3. **Operator re-orientation and hunting ($t_{\text{commit}} + \tau_{\text{blend}} \le t < t_{\text{stabilize}}$)**: Upon receiving the live manual lease ($T_{\text{lease,man}}$), the operator experiences neuromuscular latency, visual parallax, and control re-orientation, producing high-jerk, oscillatory corrections as they acquire situational awareness.
   - *Masking policy*: $\mathcal{M}(t) = 0$. Admitting these transitional frames into the imitation buffer corrupts training with human hesitation, tremors, and hunting oscillations. The stabilization boundary $t_{\text{stabilize}}$ is identified when tracking error and command slew remain below calibrated limits. In the following criterion, the inherited symbol $j_{\text{stable}}$ names the channel-specific slew threshold; it is a jerk threshold only when the command is acceleration:
   $$\|\mathbf{e}_{\text{track}}(t)\| \le \epsilon_{\text{stable}} \quad \text{and} \quad \|\dot{\mathbf{u}}_{\text{human}}(t)\| \le j_{\text{stable}} \quad \text{for } t \ge t_{\text{stabilize}}.$$

4. **Stabilized expert recovery ($t \ge t_{\text{stabilize}}$)**: The operator provides task-directed recovery guidance after the measured stabilization criteria hold. Smooth motion alone does not establish correct recovery; the episode must also satisfy the task's validity criteria before its actions become expert targets.
   - *Masking policy*: Set $\mathcal{M}(t) = 1$, with imitation target $\mathbf{u}^*(t) = \mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t)$, only for stabilized segments that also pass the task-validity review; keep other segments excluded from direct imitation. Accepted recovery trajectories expand the training distribution without treating smooth but unsuccessful intervention as expert behavior.

Feeding unsegmented logs into behavioral cloning or diffusion policies mixes synthetic enforcer ramps and operator panic into the training distribution. The mask $\mathcal{M}(t)$ and target $\mathbf{u}^*(t)$ use the safety microcontroller's authenticated PTP timestamps to distinguish controller ownership, subject to the recorded clock and sampling limits. They preserve learner-visited states for corrective relabeling while restricting imitation targets to expert relabels and reviewed recovery segments.

When assembling the safety case for operational certification, @sec-release evaluates the authority record as the evidence for claim C6, the claim that authority transfers as these four rules specify. A safety assessment examines the stated authority constraints, implementation evidence, fault coverage, and tested operating envelope. The certification package pairs the static authority manifest with the plant measurements that @sec-intervention-bumpless-transfer requires of every transfer and with execution traces from the fault-injection campaign that show any gaps in the audit trail. The plant measurements are needed because a handover that is correct at the bus can still slide the base or shift the tote rack. The measured preemption latency in those traces is a percentile of the tested distribution rather than a bound (@sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Authority records provide evidentiary artifacts for the deployment safety cases in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims.
:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls}

Changing an authority register does not complete a safe handover\index{Handover!authority register}. The machine must preserve its stopping margin\index{Safety!stopping margin} and enforcement functions\index{Enforcement!transfer boundaries} through the transfer, while the resulting logs must distinguish intervention from expert recovery\index{Imitation learning!expert recovery}.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-fixed-window-pitfall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE FIXED ACKNOWLEDGMENT WINDOW AT TWO SPEEDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls, the fixed-timeout pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one configured window fits at the crawl and overruns at
# │          the aisle speed.
# │ Show:    Travel during the window and the overrun at 1.3 m/s; the spare
# │          and T_latest at the out-of-loop crawl.
# │ How:     Finished stopping budget (jerk-limited resident stop, all
# │          overheads) at each speed, the window added to tau_delay.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionFixedWindowPitfall:
    """A configured acknowledgment window judged against the budget at two speeds."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_crawl = AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    window = InterventionTimeoutBudget.config  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    def _budget(speed, tau, a, j, ovh):
        return (speed * tau + calc_scurve_stop_distance(speed, a, j) + ovh).to(millimeter)

    budget = _budget(v, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, overhead)
    travel = (v * window).to(millimeter)
    overrun = (budget + travel - d_clear).to(millimeter)
    spare_crawl = (d_clear - _budget(v_crawl, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, overhead)).to(millimeter)
    t_latest_crawl = (spare_crawl / v_crawl).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.99) < 5e-3, f"finished budget at the aisle speed: {budget}")
    check(overrun.magnitude > 0, "The window must overrun the clear distance at the aisle speed.")
    check(t_latest_crawl > window, "The same window must fit at the crawl.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_crawl_str = fmt_velocity(v_crawl, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    window_str = fmt_latency(window, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    travel_str = fmt_length(travel, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    overrun_str = fmt_length(overrun, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_latest_crawl_str = fmt_latency(t_latest_crawl, unit=second, precision=1)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating human takeover timeout as a static time delay rather than a dynamic spatial stopping budget.*

The mobile manipulator requests a takeover at its `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.v_str` aisle speed under a configured `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.window_str` acknowledgment window\index{Handover!takeover request}. Waiting out the window before braking covers `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.travel_str`, and with the rest of the finished stopping budget the stop ends `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.overrun_str` past the `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. Before charging the missing admission delay, the same window fits at the `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.v_crawl_str` crawl, where the budget leaves `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.t_latest_crawl_str` before fallback must begin. A window that is safe in one state overruns in another, so handover timing must follow current speed, clearance, and credible deceleration, with autonomous fallback\index{Handover!autonomous fallback} beginning while the stop still fits.

**A timeout must fit the current complete stopping budget.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** At each control cycle, pair current clearance with a stopping budget containing only future delay and motion. Recompute a candidate absolute deadline and tighten the existing pending deadline when needed; recomputation must never restart its countdown. Use @eq-intervention-latest-fallback with that common origin, honor any earlier active expiry, and invoke fallback when no further wait is admissible. Do not subtract the full capture-origin delay again from clearance already reduced by that travel.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Human manual takeover should bypass automated safety barriers and grant unconstrained, open-ended actuator authority.*

The remote assistant takes over the mobile manipulator's base to route it around a pallet, and the chosen path leads toward a rack upright. Switching to human control only changes who is sending the command; it does not change the physical realities of momentum, friction, or nearby obstacles. Within this architecture, the enforcer\index{Enforcement!manual override} must continue checking the manual proposal against the admissible motion set\index{Safety!admissible motion} and constrain it when a kinodynamically feasible alternative exists (building on the feasibility principles from @sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility). If the request cannot be admitted, the defined autonomous fallback still applies. Takeover lets the operator guide the task planning; it does not make force, clearance, and stopping limits optional at the joint actuator\index{Hardware!actuator boundary} boundary.

Manual takeover also requires a bounded grant of proposal authority. Packet loss or operator distraction must not leave stale setpoints active indefinitely. The **manual lease** must fit the manual mode's stopping reserve; this example uses the `{python} InterventionTimeoutBudget.manual_lease_str` manual lease. If authenticated renewal ceases, expiration revokes manual authority and invokes the validated local fallback without waiting for the operator or application software.

**Intervention transfers the right to propose, never the right to violate physics or outlive fresh evidence.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Route all operator inputs through the enforcer's barrier certificates and kinodynamic clamping filters. If a human commands a turn that would tip the chassis or shear a gearbox, the enforcer clamps the setpoint or asserts a validated fallback stop. Bind manual authority to a hardware-timed lease sized against the active mode's stopping reserve; expiration invokes the validated braking or holding response.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-verifier-flood-pitfall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORGED PACKETS QUEUED AHEAD OF A GENUINE VETO
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls, the verifier-flooding
# │          pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that authentication alone leaves an availability hazard:
# │          forged packets that the verifier must reject still spend its time.
# │ Show:    The signature verification time per packet; the fewest forged
# │          signed takeover requests queued ahead of a genuine veto that push
# │          its admission past T_latest at the aisle speed; the admission time
# │          they cause and the arrival rate they need; the same count for
# │          MAC-only frames.
# │ How:     Serial verification on the permission processor, each signed
# │          packet taking t_sig of InterventionAuthBudget; the genuine veto
# │          finishes after (n + 1) verifications; the forgeries must arrive
# │          within that interval.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_count, check

class InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall:
    """Forged takeover packets that delay a genuine veto past T_latest."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_verify = InterventionAuthBudget.t_sig  # category: derived (sourced cycles / MCU clock)
    t_mac = InterventionAuthBudget.t_mac  # category: derived
    t_latest = InterventionTimeoutBudget.t_latest  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Fewest forged packets n with (n + 1) * t_verify > t_latest.
    n_forged = math.floor((t_latest / t_verify).to("").magnitude)
    t_admit = ((n_forged + 1) * t_verify).to(millisecond)
    # Whole packets per second the forger must sustain, rounded up.
    arrival_rate = math.ceil((n_forged / t_admit).to(1 / second).magnitude)
    n_forged_mac = math.floor((t_latest / t_mac).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_forged == 55, f"forged packets that push the veto past T_latest: {n_forged}")
    check(t_admit > t_latest, "The queued forgeries must push the veto past T_latest.")
    check(n_forged * t_verify <= t_latest, "One fewer forgery must still let the veto fit.")
    check(n_forged_mac > 100 * n_forged, "A MAC-only flood needs far more frames than a signature flood.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_verify_str = fmt_latency(t_verify, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    n_forged_str = fmt_count(n_forged)
    arrival_rate_str = fmt_int(arrival_rate)
    n_forged_mac_str = fmt_count(n_forged_mac)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying on cryptographic authentication without rate limiting the traffic that reaches the verifier.*

Consider an admission queue that checks each signed remote takeover request of @sec-intervention-authenticating-intervention, at `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_verify_str` per Ed25519 signature\index{Authentication!signature verification}. Verification rejects a forged request only after spending that time on it. If a faulty or compromised node on the link\index{Network!availability} sends signed `manual_drive` requests that fail verification faster than the verifier retires them, as few as `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_str` of them queued ahead of the remote assistant's genuine `veto_path` delay its admission to `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_admit_str`, past the `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_latest_str` fallback deadline $T_{\text{latest}}$ at the aisle speed. The forger needs to deliver only about `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.arrival_rate_str` requests per second, a rate any wireless link carries. A MAC-only stream moves the bottleneck without removing it. A MAC flood would need `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_mac_str` forged frames inside the same deadline, so the link's frame rate rather than the verifier limits it. The independently wired protective input and local lease timer do not wait in that queue. Their qualified responses must remain available even when network requests cannot be admitted. Authentication preserves command integrity while leaving an availability hazard. Mailbox filtering and per-source rate limiting\index{Network!rate limiting} must bound the traffic before it reaches the verifier, and qualification must test both command rejection and enforcement timing under the admitted load.

**Authentication preserves integrity while introducing a denial-of-service hazard: a receiver cannot prioritize authenticated packets over malicious packets without spending CPU cycles to verify them first.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Implement hardware mailbox filtering and per-source token-bucket rate limiters on fieldbus controllers before packets reach the cryptographic verification queue. Provide an out-of-band, hardwired electrical line for emergency protective stops that bypasses network verification entirely.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Training directly on raw human intervention logs captures expert demonstrations.*

A learning pipeline treats every remote-assistant takeover of the mobile manipulator as an expert demonstration\index{Imitation learning!expert demonstration} and trains on the preceding action window. In imitation learning, unsegmented takeover episodes combine genuine policy failures, cautious early interventions, and operator kinematic mistakes, while the control transition itself often includes jerky physical corrections, delayed neuromuscular responses, and hesitant hunting as the human re-acquires situational awareness. Cloning those transitional segments teaches the network to reproduce the very instability that necessitated the rescue. Dataset aggregation algorithms (such as DAgger [@ross2011reduction]) require isolating learner-visited states from expert corrective actions. Neither an intervention timestamp nor manual authority alone establishes that the recorded behavior is suitable for behavioral cloning or diffusion policy training.

**Unsegmented takeover logs teach neural policies to imitate near-failure oscillations and human panic.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Use hardware PTP commit timestamps to enforce causal intervention masking (@eq-intervention-causal-masking-loss). Segregate pre-commit data (Interval 1) for failure-mode analysis, never using the policy's own commands as targets and admitting a state only with an expert relabel as its new target, zero out the enforcer's transition phase (Interval 2, $\mathcal{M}(t)=0$), exclude the transitional re-orientation phase from imitation while retaining its raw forensic data (Interval 3, $\mathcal{M}(t)=0$), and train imitation policies only on post-stabilization manual guidance that also passes task-validity review (Interval 4, $\mathcal{M}(t)=1$).

:::

## Summary {#sec-intervention-summary}

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-summary-waiting
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WAITING BUDGET FOR THE SUMMARY AND TAKEAWAYS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-summary (first paragraph) and the chapter
# │          takeaways ("Clearance governs waiting").
# │
# │ Goal:    Restate the machine's handover deadline and takeover speeds.
# │ Show:    Spare margin and T_latest at the aisle speed; T_latest at the
# │          slow-down; the chosen slow-down and crawl speeds; the
# │          out-of-loop ceiling.
# │ How:     Finished stopping budget (jerk-limited resident stop, all
# │          overheads) from the WarehouseAisle scenario; ceilings by
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionSummaryWaiting:
    """Spare stopping margin spent as waiting time, and the takeover speeds it forces."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    t_in = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    v_in = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: chosen
    v_ool = AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: chosen
    t_latest_in = InterventionTimeoutBudget.t_latest_in  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    budget = (v * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare / v).to(millisecond)
    ceil_in = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear,
        tau_delay + t_in,
        a_brake,
        j_brake,
        AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track,
        AISLE.delta_margin,
    ).to(meter / second)
    ceil_ool = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear,
        tau_delay + t_ool,
        a_brake,
        j_brake,
        AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track,
        AISLE.delta_margin,
    ).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.01) < 5e-3, f"spare margin at the aisle speed: {spare}")
    check(abs(t_latest.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, f"T_latest at the aisle speed: {t_latest}")
    check(abs(ceil_in.magnitude - 0.8362) < 5e-5, f"in-loop takeover ceiling: {ceil_in}")
    check(abs(ceil_ool.magnitude - 0.1911) < 5e-5, f"out-of-loop takeover ceiling: {ceil_ool}")
    check(v_in < ceil_in and v_ool < ceil_ool, "The chosen request speeds must sit under their ceilings.")
    check(abs(t_latest_in.magnitude - 663.275) < 5e-3, f"T_latest at the in-loop slow-down: {t_latest_in}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_in_str = fmt_velocity(v_in, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ool_str = fmt_velocity(v_ool, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_in_str = fmt_latency(t_in, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ool_str = fmt_latency(t_ool, unit=second, precision=1)
    ceil_in_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_in, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    ceil_ool_str = fmt_velocity(ceil_ool, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_latest_in_str = fmt_latency(t_latest_in, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Human authority over an embodied physical AI system rests on a channel-specific contract that preserves a feasible local response throughout waiting, commit, blending, and manual operation. When communication stalls or software faults occur, role-specific execution leases bound authority and invoke the validated fallback without awaiting high-level software. The autonomous chunk lease and the `{python} InterventionTimeoutBudget.manual_lease_str` manual lease each have to fit the stopping budget for the active mode. Supervisory intervention arbitrates the transition between proposers while the independent enforcer checks admitted commands and executes the selected stop when a lease lapses. Network commands reach the enforcer only after capability and authentication checks, whose computational cost makes rate limiting ahead of the verifier essential, while trusted protective wiring bypasses the network entirely. On the mobile manipulator at its `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.v_str` aisle speed, the finished stopping budget leaves `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.spare_str`, which corresponds to `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_latest_str` before subtracting the unqualified $\Delta_{\text{da}}$. Only the remainder can be spent waiting before the machine dispatches its own stop. Sourced human response times, `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_in_str` for an attending in-loop operator and `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_ool_str` at the 90th percentile of out-of-loop takeover conditions, cap the request speeds at `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.ceil_in_str` and `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.ceil_ool_str`. The worked design therefore requests an in-loop takeover only after slowing to `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.v_in_str` and an out-of-loop takeover from a `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.v_ool_str` crawl or, more robustly, from standstill after an automatic stop; a newly discovered rack-end pallet requires the local stop first. Neither candidate speed is qualified until the missing delay and remaining physical premises close.

Transferring control from an active policy takes time, because replacing an admitted policy setpoint with a different human target in one $1\text{ ms}$ cycle requests a torque step. The $C^2$ bumpless authority transfer ramp\index{C2 bumpless transfer ramp@$C^2$ bumpless authority transfer ramp} instead varies an authority parameter $\alpha(t)$ smoothly from zero to one between latched command endpoints. An optional force-reflecting console needs a separate passivity and physical-limit argument for its delayed feedback loop. Its sampled implementation must respect command-rate limits and the stopping reserve of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes.

In the illustrative design, a base command blend lasts `{python} InterventionBlendBudget.T_budget_str` at any speed, because its jerk bound belongs to the load. At the `{python} InterventionBlendBudget.v0_str` in-loop takeover speed a braking blend does not fit the clearance that remains, and no smoothed braking transition under the same bounds could beat the resident stop, so the base receives the resident stop while the arm blends over `{python} InterventionBlendBudget.arm_budget_str`. Execution remains conditional on qualification of the complete delay, rounded profile, and state-matched stopping reserve. The enforcer must monitor that reserve and the plant response at every blended tick.

The **authority record** makes each intervention forensically reviewable. As the twelfth record in the record chain, it binds the static authority manifest (pairing actuator channels to authorized actors, tiers, and deadlines) with dynamic per-tick evidence tuples $\langle t_{\text{MCU}}, S_{\text{auth}}, \mathbf{x}_{\text{state}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{prop}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{enf}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{act}}, \text{ID}_{\text{operator}}, T_{\text{lease,rem}}\rangle$ that log who held authority and what was proposed, admitted, and delivered, consuming fallback rungs from the enforcement record (@sec-enforcement-telemetry) and operator-path latencies from the placement record (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation). A logged commit marks the recorded boundary where autonomous policy authority was revoked, subject to the logger's clock and sampling limits, and hash chaining with protected keys can reveal later modification. Command and authority records support reconstruction only when paired with independent sensor, current, and contact evidence and their timing uncertainty.

For model training, the pre-commit interval is a **policy-owned** segment even when a human is deciding to intervene. Retain its learner-visited states, unsafe proposals, and authority flags as failure evidence and candidates for expert relabeling; exclude unsafe policy commands from expert imitation targets. The post-commit blend is enforcer-owned transition data. Only reviewed post-transfer human recovery states and actions that meet the task's validity criteria should become demonstrations.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Supervisory intervention and authority bounds"}
* **State-dependent fallback and monotonic leases:** Bind each proposer to its mode-specific lease and stopping reserve. Expiry invokes the validated local response for the current state, with the sensing, drive energy, braking, and holding premises that response requires. The manual lease here is `{python} InterventionTimeoutBudget.manual_lease_str`.
* **Clearance governs waiting:** The partial budget gives `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_latest_str` at aisle speed and `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_latest_in_str` at the `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.v_in_str` candidate slow-down. Subtract the missing $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ in that capture-origin ledger. Live checks pair current clearance with only future delay and obey earlier active expiry. Price the human at a sourced percentile, not a hopeful point value. A `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_in_str` in-loop response needs a speed below `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.ceil_in_str`, and a `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.t_ool_str` out-of-loop takeover a speed below `{python} InterventionSummaryWaiting.ceil_ool_str`, which makes stopping before handover the robust design. Dispatch fallback by the earlier of the configuration ceiling and the state-dependent stopping deadline.
* **One actuator writer:** Source arbitration and exclusive enforcer output ownership prevent conflicting actuator writes; bus arbitration alone does not establish authority. The four-phase takeover protocol (Request, Acknowledge, Commit, Confirm) shifts authority deterministically. Commit revokes the policy's token on the committed channels and latches its last admitted command. The enforcer owns `BLEND` and checks human proposals against the same physical limits before releasing the supervisory token.
* **Smooth commands and haptic passivity:** A fixed-endpoint $C^2$ acceleration profile bounds commanded jerk during transfer, and its extra stopping distance must be reserved. An optional bilateral console also needs qualified interaction-energy control under its stated delay, loss, and actuator assumptions.
* **Distinct stop paths:** Trusted protective wiring invokes a risk-assessed plant response. Invalid network packets are rejected; lost valid renewal invokes the lease fallback.
* **Causal intervention data:** Enforce the four-interval causal mask $\mathcal{M}(t)$ (@eq-intervention-causal-masking-loss). Retain learner-visited drift states for DAgger relabeling, zero out synthetic enforcer splines ($\tau_{\text{blend}}$) and operator re-orientation hunting, and admit only stabilized, task-validity-reviewed human recovery trajectories into imitation training buffers.
* **Authority becomes evidence:** The authority record logs per-tick evidence tuples $\langle t_{\text{MCU}}, S_{\text{auth}}, \mathbf{x}_{\text{state}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{prop}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{enf}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{act}}, \text{ID}_{\text{operator}}, T_{\text{lease,rem}}\rangle$ into tamper-evident hash chains, treating a missing entry as a gap, never an implied pass. The manifest's four authority rules become the fault cases verification injects, and their passing records, with the authority record, provide the formal evidence for release claim C6.
:::

A person's authority over the machine is granted on evidence and expires with it, as principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority} requires of every authority the machine honors. The credential and the committed handshake are the evidence that grants it; the manual lease is that evidence's age limit, and when the operator's input stops renewing it, the authority strictly lapses to a safe fallback the permission path owns. A preemption tier does not survive the lapse, and the remote assistant who held the base before it holds no authority after it. Returning control to any proposer waits on the reset conditions the state machine specifies, and on fresh evidence.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From authority revocation to verification"}
Does a clean authority log show that the authority rules hold? It does not, because no logged handover exercised the duplicate writer, the replayed packet, or the unacknowledged request that the rules exist to contain. @Sec-verification turns A1–A4 into fault cases beside the rack-end faults, injects each with the loaded base approaching the rack end, and times each response with instruments independent of the machine's own log, so that request, commit, response onset, and stopping completion are measured as distinct events rather than inferred from the arbiter's log.
:::
